events.description: The Greco-Persian Wars (499–449 BCE) were fifty years of intermittent conflict between the Greek city-states and the Achaemenid Persian Empire, starting with the failed Ionian Revolt and ending after Greek victories at Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The wars began when Persian king Cyrus the Great absorbed the Greek-inhabited region of Ionia (the Aegean coast of modern Turkey) in 547 BCE and installed puppet tyrants over the Greek cities there — the resulting resentment eventually exploded into the Ionian Revolt of 499 BCE, which Athens and Eretria supported with ships. Persia's two full invasions of Greece (490 and 480 BCE) failed, but the conflict permanently forged a shared Greek identity around the idea of "Greek freedom" versus "Persian despotism," an identity Alexander explicitly invoked when he launched his own invasion 150 years later.

events.label: Xerxes Invades Greece
events.description: In 480 BCE, Xerxes I marched the largest army the ancient world had ever seen across a bridge of boats over the Hellespont strait, intent on finishing what his father Darius had started: the conquest of Greece.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Herodotus claimed 1.7 million soldiers — a number modern historians consider wildly inflated; realistic estimates range from 70,000 to 300,000 troops, plus 600 to 1,200 warships. Xerxes spent several years of preparation after Darius died in 486 BCE, including engineering a pontoon bridge of boats across the Hellespont that was reportedly destroyed by a storm and had to be rebuilt. Only about a tenth of all Greek city-states joined the resistance; the majority either stayed neutral or submitted to Persia outright.

events.label: Delian Treasury Moved to Athens
events.description: In 454 BCE, Athens moved the Delian League's treasury from the sacred island of Delos to Athens itself, turning an anti-Persian alliance into an Athenian cash register. The official reason was 'safekeeping'; the real reason was control.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The move followed a costly Athenian military disaster in Egypt, which gave Pericles a plausible security rationale. Once in Athens, the tribute was carved in stone on the Athenian Acropolis — surviving inscription fragments show the annual 'first-fruits' paid to Athena, a one-sixtieth tax on collected tribute that effectively made the goddess a partner in the empire. The treasury's arrival in Athens is the moment historians mark as the League's transformation into a full empire.

events.label: Corinthian War
events.description: Former Spartan allies — Athens, Thebes, Corinth, and Argos — turned on Sparta within a decade of its victory in the Peloponnesian War, fed up with Spartan arrogance and heavy-handed rule. The war ended with the King's Peace of 387 BCE, a humiliating settlement dictated by Persia that handed Greek cities in Asia Minor back to Persian control.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Persia switched sides mid-war: it initially bankrolled the anti-Spartan coalition, then pivoted to backing Sparta once Athens started rebuilding a fleet that threatened Persian Aegean interests. The war erupted while the Spartan king Agesilaus II was away campaigning in Asia against Persia — his own allies exploited his absence to open a second front at home. The King's Peace was also called the Peace of Antalcidas after the Spartan diplomat who negotiated it, giving a Spartan's name to a treaty that handed Greek autonomy to Persia.

events.label: Olympic Truce Tradition
events.description: Before each Olympic Games, heralds fanned out across the Greek world to announce the ekecheiria (sacred truce), suspending all warfare so athletes and spectators could travel safely to and from Olympia. It was the one institution that could, in theory, pause Greek city-states from killing each other.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The truce protected the host region of Elis and the roads to Olympia, not all of Greece — active wars elsewhere were technically allowed to continue, though participants were expected to let travelers pass unmolested. Violations of the truce were taken seriously: Sparta was famously fined and barred from competing at one Olympiad for attacking a fort during the sacred period. The modern Olympic truce, revived by the UN in 1993, is a direct callback to this ancient institution.

events.label: Minoan Civilization
events.description: The Minoan civilization on Crete was Europe first advanced civilization, with elaborate palaces at Knossos, sophisticated frescoes, and widespread Mediterranean trade. Its collapse around 1450 BCE opened the way for Mycenaean dominance.

events.label: Mycenaean Civilization
events.description: The Bronze Age palace civilization of mainland Greece (roughly 1750–1050 BCE), centered on fortified citadels at Mycenae, Tiryns, and Pylos. They ran palace economies, traded across the eastern Mediterranean, and left behind the earliest known Greek writing (Linear B clay tablets).

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mycenaean palace bureaucrats tracked inventories of sheep, weapons, and oil on clay tablets in Linear B — a syllabic script that would vanish entirely with the palace collapse around 1200 BCE, leaving Greece illiterate for three centuries. At their peak, Mycenaean settlements extended as far as Cyprus, the Levant, and southern Italy. The famous gold 'Mask of Agamemnon' found at Mycenae by Heinrich Schliemann in 1876 actually predates any historical Agamemnon by three centuries.

events.label: Trojan War (traditional)
events.description: The legendary war between the Mycenaean Greeks and Troy, immortalized in Homer Iliad. Whether a real conflict lies behind the myth remains debated, but it shaped Greek identity and literature for centuries.

events.label: Long Walls of Athens
events.description: The Long Walls were two parallel fortification corridors connecting Athens to its port at Piraeus (about 4 miles / 6.5 km apart), turning the city into an island on land — attackers could burn every farm in Attica and Athens would still receive grain ships and stay fed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The walls were first built in the 460s BCE and were one of the main reasons Sparta's strategy of annual land invasions could never force Athens to surrender on its own terms. The Corinthians and Thebans reportedly wanted Athens razed entirely in 404 BCE; Sparta blocked that but insisted the walls be demolished. When Athens recovered, it rebuilt them in the 390s BCE — Sparta accepted this because they needed Athenian help against Thebes.

events.label: Empedocles
events.description: Empedocles (roughly 490–430 BCE) proposed that everything in the universe is made of four elements — earth, water, air, and fire — pushed together and pulled apart by forces he called Love and Strife. His model dominated Western natural philosophy for nearly 2,000 years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Empedocles was from Akragas in Sicily, not mainland Greece, and was a figure of almost legendary strangeness in antiquity: he reportedly wore a golden crown and bronze sandals, and the story (almost certainly apocryphal) goes that he threw himself into Mount Etna to prove he was a god. More verifiably, he proposed an early version of evolutionary thinking — creatures with poorly combined parts perished, while better-combined ones survived, a rough foreshadowing of natural selection. His four-element theory was the framework Hippocrates used for humoral medicine.
